Cross-tenant RabbitMQ queue/exchange enumeration via management API (CVE-2026-57221) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts a single source enumerating many queue and exchange names through the RabbitMQ management API (/api/queues, /api/exchanges) on port 15672, abusing the missing authorization that lets any connected vhost user read all queue/exchange names, message counts and consumer counts regardless of permissions. Rationale: Uses the specific management API resource paths (/api/queues, /api/exchanges) and port 15672 tied to the missing-authz flaw; a source pulling >20 distinct queue/exchange paths in a short window is the enumeration behaviour the CVE enables, whereas normal management UI use touches few endpoints.
ATT&CKT1087 T1580
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • RabbitMQ management UI overview page auto-refreshing and paging through the full queue/exchange list for a legitimate admin
  • Monitoring exporters (rabbitmq_exporter / Prometheus) scraping /api/queues and /api/exchanges on a schedule
  • Capacity/inventory tooling walking all vhosts for reporting
  • CI pipelines validating broker topology across many queues
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("monitoring-host-ip-not-known") and not (ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr) and DstHostname has "exporter")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the authenticated user behind SrcIpAddr and compare their assigned vhost permissions to the breadth of queues/exchanges enumerated; legit monitoring accounts are expected, ad-hoc user accounts are not. 2) Contain: restrict port 15672 to trusted management networks, separate tenants by vhost, and patch to the fixed release lines. 3) Hunt: review whether the same principal then consumed messages or authenticated to queues outside its tenant, and correlate with any /api/auth secret-leak hits.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where HttpMethod == "GET"
| where DstPortNumber == 15672 or Url has ":15672"
| where Url has_any ("/api/queues", "/api/exchanges")
| summarize RequestCount = count(), DistinctPaths = dcount(Url), SampledPaths = make_set(Url, 50), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname
| where DistinctPaths > 20   // bulk queue/exchange name enumeration in one window
| order by DistinctPaths desc
APPLICATION

| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=GET Web.dest_port=15672 (Web.uri_path="/api/queues*" OR Web.uri_path="/api/exchanges*") by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.uri_path
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| stats dc(uri_path) as distinctPaths sum(count) as totalRequests values(uri_path) as sampledPaths by src, dest
| where distinctPaths > 20
| sort - distinctPaths
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=GET Web.dest_port=15672 (Web.uri_path="/api/queues*" OR Web.uri_path="/api/exchanges*") by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.uri_path
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| stats dc(uri_path) as distinctPaths sum(count) as totalRequests values(uri_path) as sampledPaths by src, dest

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-57219", "CVE-2026-57221")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.

11 Old Microsoft-Signed Linux UEFI Shims Could Let Attackers Bypass Secure Boot

The Hacker News
2026-07-14 5 use cases 2 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have discovered 11 old, Microsoft-signed, Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) applications that could be abused to bypass Secure Boot on most systems using the modern firmware standard. "An attacker exploiting one of these vulnerable applications can execute untrusted code during system boot, enabling deployment of malicious UEFI bootkits or other malware,"

Revoked Microsoft-signed vulnerable UEFI shim present in estate (CVE-2026-8863 / CVE-2026-10797) AIInstallation High
Surfaces hosts carrying one of the 11 old Microsoft-signed shim bootloaders (shim 0.9 and earlier) revoked in Microsoft's June 2026 DBX update. Any device still exposing CVE-2026-8863 or CVE-2026-10797 can be used to bypass UEFI Secure Boot by bringing the still-trusted-but-unrevoked binary, so this is an exposure hunt, not a live-exploit alert. Rationale: Uses the two concrete CVE IDs assigned to the 11 revoked shims (confirmed by ESET/CERT). A pure inventory lookup — zero behavioural noise, ideal for prioritising DBX/fwupd remediation on Linux fleets that trust the Microsoft Corporation UEFI CA 2011 cert. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/forgotten-uefi-shims-undermining-secure-boot/ • https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/457458 • https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/616257
ATT&CKT1542.003 T1553.006
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Air-gapped/offline lab boxes intentionally kept on old shims for reproduction
  • Appliances (Blancco WipeDrive / PC-Doctor / baramundi) that legitimately ship the affected shim as designed
  • Hosts pending a scheduled fwupd/DBX maintenance window
  • Golden images not yet re-baked after the June 2026 revocation
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the device trusts the Microsoft 3rd-party CA and check `mokutil --sb-state` and DBX entry count (`efi-readvar -v dbx | grep -c sha256`, expect 200+). 2) Contain: push the Microsoft June-2026 DBX/fwupd revocation update or apply the SBAT level bump so the old shim can no longer load; prioritise internet-facing and privileged-user hosts. 3) Hunt: on any host that resisted DBX update, pivot to UC2/UC3 to check whether the ESP shim was actually swapped or MOK/SBAT validation was disabled.

Old shim/GRUB EFI binary written to ESP by non-package-manager process (Secure Boot bypass staging) AIInstallation Medium
Detects writes of a shim, MokManager or GRUB EFI binary into the EFI System Partition by a process that is NOT a legitimate package manager / firmware updater. This is the core of the attack: replacing the victim's up-to-date shim with an older, still-Microsoft-signed vulnerable one to reintroduce a bootkit-capable early-boot code-exec path that survives OS reinstall. Rationale: Anchors on the exact ESP artifact names (shimx64.efi / mmx64.efi / grubx64.efi) and the /boot/efi path where an attacker swaps in the old signed shim; excluding real installers/fwupd keeps the true-positive (manual/scripted replacement) sharp. ESET's core finding is that only 'a copy of an old still-trusted shim' is needed. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/forgotten-uefi-shims-undermining-secure-boot/ • https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/457458
ATT&CKT1542.003 T1542.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Distro kernel/shim upgrade run via a wrapper the exclusion list misses (e.g. ansible/salt invoking cp directly)
  • Imaging/provisioning tools (baramundi, FOG) legitimately writing shim to ESP during deployment
  • Manual `cp`/`dd` by a sysadmin recovering an unbootable machine
  • Dual-boot setup utilities re-installing the EFI bootloader
  • Backup/restore agents rehydrating /boot/efi
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "ansible" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("salt-minion","puppet","chef-client","cloud-init")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the written binary's SHA256 and compare against the distro's current signed shim; run `objdump -j .sbat -s <file>` — an absent/low-generation .sbat section on a freshly written shim is a strong signal of an old vulnerable build. Confirm the writing process/user was not a package transaction. 2) Contain: isolate the host, restore the vendor-current shim, and (re)apply the DBX revocation so the old binary can't load; reset boot order with efibootmgr. 3) Hunt: check UC3 for accompanying `mokutil --disable-validation`/SBAT reset, and scan other hosts for the same file hash and writing-process lineage.

| where FileName in~ ("shimx64.efi","shimaa64.efi","shimia32.efi","mmx64.efi","grubx64.efi","fbx64.efi","bootx64.efi")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("dpkg","rpm","apt","apt-get","dnf","yum","zypper","zypp","fwupd","fwupdmgr","grub-install","grub2-install","shim-install","update-grub","packagekitd")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Old Vulnerable Shim/GRUB EFI Binary Written to ESP by Non-Installer
id: 5c2f8a41-9b6e-4d13-8a77-2e1c4b90d6f2
description: Detects a shim/MokManager/GRUB EFI binary written into /boot/efi by a process that is not a legitimate package manager or firmware updater, consistent with staging an older Microsoft-signed vulnerable shim to bypass Secure Boot (CVE-2026-8863 / CVE-2026-10797).
references:
  - https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/forgotten-uefi-shims-undermining-secure-boot/
  - https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/457458
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/14
tags:
  - attack.t1542.003
  - attack.t1542.001
  - attack.defense_evasion
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: linux
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|contains: '/boot/efi/'
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - 'shimx64.efi'
      - 'shimaa64.efi'
      - 'mmx64.efi'
      - 'grubx64.efi'
      - 'fbx64.efi'
      - 'bootx64.efi'
  filter_installer:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/dpkg'
      - '/rpm'
      - '/apt'
      - '/dnf'
      - '/yum'
      - '/zypper'
      - '/fwupd'
      - '/grub-install'
      - '/grub2-install'
      - '/shim-install'
      - '/update-grub'
  condition: selection and not filter_installer
level: high
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\/boot\/efi\/.*(shimx64|shimaa64|shimia32|mmx64|grubx64|fbx64|bootx64)\.efi$/i
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/\/(dpkg|rpm|apt|apt-get|dnf|yum|zypper|fwupd|fwupdmgr|grub2?-install|shim-install|update-grub)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Endpoint.file_name IN ("shimx64.efi","shimaa64.efi","shimia32.efi","mmx64.efi","grubx64.efi","fbx64.efi","bootx64.efi") Endpoint.file_path="*/boot/efi/*" NOT Endpoint.process_name IN ("dpkg","rpm","apt","apt-get","dnf","yum","zypper","fwupd","fwupdmgr","grub-install","grub2-install","shim-install","update-grub") by Endpoint.dest, Endpoint.file_name, Endpoint.file_path, Endpoint.process_name, Endpoint.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Endpoint)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Endpoint.file_name IN ("shimx64.efi","shimaa64.efi","shimia32.efi","mmx64.efi","grubx64.efi","fbx64.efi","bootx64.efi") Endpoint.file_path="*/boot/efi/*" NOT Endpoint.process_name IN ("dpkg","rpm","apt","apt-get","dnf","yum","zypper","fwupd","fwupdmgr","grub-install","grub2-install","shim-install","update-grub") by Endpoint.dest, Endpoint.file_name, Endpoint.file_path, Endpoint.process_name, Endpoint.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Endpoint)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
MOK/SBAT enforcement disabled via mokutil (Secure Boot validation subversion) AIInstallation Medium
Detects mokutil invocations that disable shim signature validation or roll back the SBAT revocation policy — the exact levers the article describes for bypassing MOK-denylist and SBAT enforcement so an older revoked shim will load unchallenged. Pairs with UC2 to catch the enforcement-weakening half of the chain. Rationale: The article states the bypass works by defeating MOK-denylist and SBAT enforcement; `mokutil --disable-validation` and `--set-sbat-policy` (with `--import`/`--reset`) are the precise CLI levers to do that (corroborated by shim/mokutil docs). Named binary + dangerous flags keeps it targeted rather than a generic 'mokutil ran' dashboard. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/forgotten-uefi-shims-undermining-secure-boot/ • https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/616257
ATT&CKT1553.006 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin enrolling a new MOK for a third-party/DKMS driver (`mokutil --import`)
  • Sanctioned SBAT policy rollback during a distro-support troubleshooting case
  • NVIDIA/VirtualBox/DKMS module signing workflows on first install
  • Golden-image build pipelines enrolling keys before hardening
  • Lab/test hosts where an engineer disabled validation intentionally
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("dkms","akmods","packagekitd") and ProcessCommandLine has "--import")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the invoking user/parent is an expected admin/automation account and whether a DKMS/third-party driver install is in flight; `--disable-validation` and SBAT `--reset` outside a change window are the red flags. 2) Contain: re-enable validation (`mokutil --enable-validation`), restore the current SBAT level, and revoke any unexpected enrolled MOK; isolate if paired with an ESP shim write (UC2). 3) Hunt: correlate on the same host for a recent shim/GRUB EFI write (UC2), new efibootmgr boot-order changes, and reboots shortly after; sweep the fleet for the same command lineage.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "mokutil"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--disable-validation", "--set-sbat-policy", "--import", "--reset")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "mokutil"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("--disable-validation", "--set-sbat-policy", "--import", "--reset")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
